policy_title: Prioritise restorative justice and rehabilitation over short prison sentences
stated: Expand restorative justice and legislate for a presumption against custodial sentences under two years to reduce reoffending. Implement diversion programmes for low-level drug and alcohol offences and young offenders, focusing on rehabilitation through investment in probation and prison services.

source.quote: Green MPs will expand restorative justice when crimes do take place, both to give victims a voice and to help offenders take responsibility for the harm they have done. Elected Greens will seek to break the cycle of reoffending through legislating for a presumption against custodial sentences under two years. Elected Greens will ensure that diversion programmes are in place for: • All low-level drug and alcohol related offences. • Young offenders arrested for low-level offences.

bearing_set.reason: Directly reshapes sentencing (presumption against <2-year custodial), reoffending rates, probation and prison capacity, and diversion from the criminal justice system — all core O5 indicators.

A statutory presumption against custodial sentences under two years directly reduces the frequency with which the state incarcerates individuals, expanding personal liberty for a large category of offenders; diversion programmes similarly substitute coercion for engagement — a concrete, non-negligible improvement to freedom from state coercion.

The policy combines an explicit spending commitment ('investment in probation and prison services') with a mechanism that would reduce the prison population (short sentences avoided) and thus prison running costs (~£47k/prisoner/year UK); the net fiscal effect is real and contested in direction, clearing the non-negligible bar for public-finances sustainability.

membership_note: Core bearing-set is the justice/safety tradeoff (O5), the liberty gain from reduced custody (O10), and the material but directionally-contested fiscal effect of the investment vs prison-cost-saving (O12). Effects on inequality (O14) or equal treatment (O9) are real but incidental — the policy is not specifically anti-discrimination and the distributional effects do not independently drive a non-negligible verdict on those fundamentals.
